open-question.question: Does the new tool mirror the open-question tool's stream and exit-status contract (one Error: line on stderr with exit 1, argparse usage with exit 2, empty stdout on failure, never a traceback)?
open-question.recommendation: Copying the stream reconfiguration and the three exception clauses gives both tools one identical contract (one folded Error: line on stderr, exit 1, argparse exit 2, empty stdout on failure, never a traceback) and lets test_contract.py's assertions be reused as they are; the error handling inside the open-question tool's main is not a separable helper, so sharing it would mean refactoring the existing tool, and distinct exit codes would be surface no skill ever branches on.
open-question.alternative: Give define_milestone.py its own main() and _fail() modelled on open_questions.py. It reconfigures stdout and stderr to UTF-8, maps ToolError and OSError to one folded Error: line on stderr with exit 1, and catches every other exception the same way so no traceback ever escapes. argparse keeps its usage message and exit 2, and stdout stays empty on every failure path. Both tools behave the same to every caller. The skill stops on an Error: line in both, test_contract.py's assertions can be copied into a sibling test file as they are, and the stdout-empty-on-failure rule means a partial success print (a subject or paths from the success output) can never reach the commit procedure after a failed run. The roughly fifteen lines of stream and exception handling exist twice, in two modules, with nothing that enforces they stay the same. If one tool's contract changes later (a new OSError folding rule, for example), the other can silently drift unless a test pins both.

Keep the contract exactly the same, but have define_milestone.py take the error-mapping entry point (the _fail helper and the ToolError/OSError/Exception handling in main) from open_questions.py instead of writing its own. The two tools then share one implementation of the stream and exit-status rules. By construction the contract cannot drift between the tools: one code path decides how an error is folded into a single line and which exit status it gets, so an OSError raised by the milestone scan reads the same as one raised inside create. This only works if the new tool imports the open-question module. If that reuse is done by running open_questions.py create as a subprocess instead, this option falls away. It also turns a private helper (_fail) and main's internals into an interface the second tool depends on, when the module docstring currently describes open_questions.xml as the one file this module owns.

alternative.id: Distinct exit status per failure class

open-question.alternative: Keep the streams the same (one Error: line on stderr, empty stdout on failure, argparse exit 2, never a traceback), but give each class of refusal its own non-zero status. For example: 1 for a conflict or invalid input, and a separate code for an I/O failure or for a failed cleanup that left files on disk. A headless chain (claude -p in ways-of-using-cairn.md) or a script could tell a harmless refusal, where nothing was written, from a case where the "leaves nothing behind" promise was broken, without parsing the Error: text. That distinction matters most when cleanup itself fails. It breaks the plugin's single tool contract and the rule every skill follows today of stopping on the Error: line whatever the status. The skill layer would never branch on the extra codes, so they are untested surface. How much they are worth depends on what the tool reports when cleanup fails, which is decided elsewhere.

open-question.question: Is the goal text read from stdin written under the Goal heading verbatim (newlines and blank lines preserved) or normalized, and is an empty, terminal, or non-UTF-8 stdin refused as the open-question tool refuses it?
open-question.recommendation: Milestones 06 and 11 already carry multi-paragraph goals with emphasis and backticks, and the skill's plain substitution keeps such text intact today, so the tool writes stdin verbatim with only the ends trimmed and applies the open-question tool's stdin refusals plus an empty-text refusal; folding would flatten those goals into one paragraph, a heading guard would reject legitimate goals that modify-milestone-goal accepts anyway, and light normalization can silently change Markdown meaning.
open-question.alternative: Write the stdin text under `## Goal` exactly as received: interior newlines, blank lines and Markdown are kept byte for byte, and only leading and trailing whitespace is trimmed, so the heredoc's final newline does not add a blank line before `## Relevant starting state`. Terminal, closed and non-UTF-8 stdin are refused with the same `read_body` rules the open-question tool uses, and empty or whitespace-only text is refused with its own `Error:` line. Keeps multi-paragraph goals intact. Milestones 06 and 11 already have four- and five-paragraph goals with bold text and backticks. The template's plain substitution of `<overall_goal_description>` also has this behaviour today, so the change keeps what the skill does now while its stdin refusals match the open-question tool's. Nothing stops the goal from carrying a line that starts with `## `. Such a line opens a new section in `requirements.md` and can confuse the skills that find `## Goal`, `## Decisions` and the other sections by their headings. Sharing `read_body` rather than copying it also depends on how the new tool reaches the open-question tool's code.

Run the goal through the open-question tool's `fold` (every run of whitespace and newlines becomes one space, ends trimmed) and write it as a single paragraph. This is the same normalization and empty-after-fold refusal `add` applies to question text, alongside the same `read_body` refusals for terminal, closed and non-UTF-8 stdin. Reuses one existing, tested rule from the open-question tool, so the output is fully predictable and cannot add a heading, list or stray blank line to `requirements.md`. Destroys paragraph breaks, lists and code blocks. Multi-paragraph goals like those of milestones 06 and 11 would be merged into one wall of text, a step back from what the skill writes today.

Keep the text verbatim with the ends trimmed, as in the first option, and also refuse with one `Error:` line any goal that has a line starting with a Markdown heading marker at the section level or above (`#` or `##`). Stdin is refused on the same `read_body` grounds as the open-question tool, and empty text is refused too. Keeps multi-paragraph goals while making sure the file's section structure, which later skills rely on to find and edit sections, cannot be broken by the goal text. Adds a refusal rule that must be specified and tested, and it rejects some legitimate goals, such as ones quoting a heading or using a `##` sub-heading. The model then has to rewrite the goal and call the tool again. `modify-milestone-goal` also edits `## Goal` without that guard, so the rule would hold only at definition time.

Keep the paragraph structure but tidy it mechanically. CRLF line endings become LF, trailing whitespace is stripped from each line, runs of blank lines collapse to one, and the ends are trimmed. Stdin is refused on the same `read_body` grounds, and text left empty after normalization is refused too. Gives clean, consistent Markdown whatever the shell, editor or headless caller produced, while keeping the paragraphs, lists and emphasis that folding would lose. The output is no longer verbatim, and every rule needs its own specification and tests. Removing trailing whitespace can quietly change meaning, because two trailing spaces in Markdown are a hard line break and whitespace inside a fenced code block may matter.

open-question.question: Does the skill keep its single goal-description argument with the model deriving the title from it, or take a separate title argument, and does the headless invocation in ways-of-using-cairn.md change accordingly?
open-question.recommendation: The goal itself assigns choosing the title to the model as the skill's one remaining judgment, and keeping the single goal argument leaves the headless line, the discuss-milestone-goal handoff, the skill reference and CONTRIBUTING untouched; a required title argument would break every existing invocation and contradict the goal, and an optional prefix would give the skill two modes and a delimiter-detection rule.
open-question.alternative: Keep the single `<overall_goal_description>` argument. The model reads it, picks a title, and passes that title to the tool as `--title`, with the goal text on stdin. `docs/ways-of-using-cairn.md`, the `discuss-milestone-goal` handoff, `docs/skill-reference.md` and `CONTRIBUTING.md` stay as they are. This is what the Goal already describes ("the model's only work in the skill is choosing the title"). No call site changes, so the headless `claude -p "/cairn:define-milestone-goal <goal>"` line and every handoff that suggests `/define-milestone-goal "<refined goal>"` keep working as they are. The title fixes the slug, and the slug fixes the milestone id. That makes the directory name model-chosen and not repeatable, so a headless chain still can't know `<milestone_id>` before the run. It also keeps today's inconsistency, where the 37 existing headings mix Title Case and sentence case, unless the skill adds a rule for the title's form.

Add a required title to the invocation, for example `/define-milestone-goal <title>. <goal>`, split on the first `.` the way `answer-open-question` already splits its argument. The skill passes the title to `--title` word for word. The headless line in `docs/ways-of-using-cairn.md`, its placeholder legend, the `discuss-milestone-goal` handoff and the `docs/skill-reference.md` heading all change to the two-part form. The model no longer chooses anything, so the skill is fully mechanical. The user or chain author fixes the title, and with it the slug, before the run. The setup chain's `<milestone_id>` becomes predictable from what was passed, apart from the scanned number, and headings follow one convention because a person wrote them. It changes a documented interface across several sites, and every existing invocation that passes only a goal would break or be misread. It also goes against the Goal's statement that the model chooses the title, so the Goal would need revising. A title that itself contains the delimiter can't be expressed without an escape rule.

Keep the goal-only form as the default and also accept an optional leading title marked by a fixed delimiter, such as a first line or a `<title>.` prefix. The skill passes that title word for word when it is present and has the model derive one when it is absent. `docs/ways-of-using-cairn.md` keeps its line and gains, at most, a note on the explicit form. Existing invocations and handoffs stay valid, and anyone who wants a repeatable milestone id, such as a headless chain or the maintainer reserving a contributor's milestone, can still pin the title. The Goal's statement that the model chooses the title stays true for the default path. The skill gets two modes, plus a parsing rule for recognising whether a title was given. A goal that happens to start in the delimited shape would be split by mistake. The default path keeps the model-chosen, non-repeatable directory name, so the determinism is only there for users who ask for it.

open-question.question: Does the new tool get its own pytest coverage under tests/ following the existing per-subcommand convention, with a second subprocess runner fixture in conftest.py and fixtures for milestone-root layouts, run under both interpreters and in CI?
open-question.recommendation: Flat per-concern files with a run_define fixture and a layout helper beside run_tool in conftest.py follow the suite's existing rule of one file per unit of behaviour, give each rule of the goal (number, slug, conflict, cleanup, output) a named home instead of one file that grows as test_embed.py did, and are collected by both interpreter runs and CI with no configuration change, whereas a subdirectory departs from the flat layout and forces distinct basenames or __init__.py files.
open-question.alternative: Add several flat test files beside the existing ones, one per concern of the new tool (for example numbering and padding, slug derivation, conflicts, failure cleanup, output and exit contract). conftest.py gets a second pinned path and a `run_define` subprocess fixture next to `run_tool`, plus a helper that builds milestone-root layouts under `tmp_path`. Because pytest's `testpaths = ["tests"]` and the `core/tools` pythonpath already cover the new files, both interpreter runs and the drift-gate job pick them up with no change to the workflow. It follows the suite's existing rule of one file per unit of behaviour and its shared-fixture pattern, so each rule in the milestone goal (number, slug, conflict, leave nothing behind, printed subject and paths) gets its own clearly named home. It costs nothing in CI and is covered at the 3.9 floor automatically. The new tool has one command and no subcommands, so the "one file per subcommand" convention does not carry over directly and the split has to be invented. conftest.py then serves two tools under a docstring written for one. The file boundaries also depend on how the sibling questions settle the tool's rules (slug normalization, conflict definition, cleanup scope), so they may need redrawing.

Put all coverage of the new tool in one `tests/test_define_milestone.py`, matching the tool's single command. Its subprocess runner and milestone-root layout helpers are defined as fixtures local to that file, and conftest.py stays untouched apart from anything both tools need, such as the shared `sys.dont_write_bytecode` guard, which already applies. CI and both interpreter runs pick up the file with no change. It maps one tool with one command onto one test file, the closest reading of the per-subcommand convention. conftest.py keeps its single-tool purpose, and the whole new surface can be reviewed or removed as one unit. The file will likely grow large, as `test_embed.py` did at over 1,300 lines, because it collects every rule of numbering, slugging, conflicts, cleanup, and output in one place. Contract checks that parallel `test_contract.py` (one `Error:` line, exit 1, argparse exit 2, no traceback) end up duplicated in shape rather than shared.

Create a `tests/define_milestone/` subtree with its own conftest.py holding the new tool's runner and layout fixtures, and its own test files split by concern. The existing open-question suite stays flat and unchanged. The subtree is collected through `testpaths` in both interpreter runs and in CI. It gives each tool its own fixture namespace and its own place, so neither suite's fixtures or docstrings have to accommodate the other. It also scales cleanly if more tools join `core/tools/` later. The directory layout of the suite departs from its established flat per-file convention. Pytest's rootdir-relative module naming means test files that share a basename across the two trees would need `__init__.py` files or distinct names. Documentation that describes `tests/` as "one test_<subcommand>.py per concern" would also need rewording.

open-question.question: Which surfaces that describe the plugin as shipping one Python tool (CLAUDE.md, CONTRIBUTING.md, the bootstrap's Python-check justification, docs/skill-reference.md, docs/workflow.md) are updated to name the second tool, and how?
open-question.recommendation: Rewording every count phrase to the plugin's stdlib-only Python tools under tools/ fixes each statement the second tool makes false, including the bootstrap's prerequisite justification, without fixing the number two into prose that a third tool would make stale again; the define tool is then named only where its behaviour is described (the CLAUDE.md layout line and the skill reference entry), and the sole-writer parenthetical is reworded rather than dropped.
open-question.alternative: Replace each phrase that states a count ("one stdlib-only Python tool", "the one program", the bootstrap justification that names only `open_questions.py`) with wording that doesn't count, such as "the plugin's stdlib-only Python tools under `tools/`". Name `define_milestone.py` only where its behaviour is actually described: the CLAUDE.md layout line and the `define-milestone-goal` entry in docs/skill-reference.md. The wording stays true when another tool is added later. Each surface carries only what its reader needs: the Python prerequisite is about "the plugin's tools", and only the per-skill reference describes what the define tool does. The general phrasing tells a reader less. CONTRIBUTING.md and the bootstrap no longer point at a specific file to run or test. The CLAUDE.md opening sentence also loses its parenthetical about the open-question tool being the sole writer of its document, unless that parenthetical is reworded rather than dropped.

Edit every listed surface to name `core/tools/define_milestone.py` next to the open-question tool. That means the CLAUDE.md opening sentence, its layout block (a second `core/tools/` line) and a new invariant bullet for the define tool; CONTRIBUTING.md's "the one program" becomes "two programs"; the bootstrap's Python-check justification names both `python3 {{PLUGIN_ROOT}}/tools/...` commands; the `define-milestone-goal` entry in docs/skill-reference.md is rewritten around the tool; and docs/workflow.md's definition phase says the tool writes all four files. README.md's prerequisite sentence gets the same change. Afterwards no surface undercounts or misdescribes the shipped tools. Readers of the bootstrap check and the contributor guide learn about the second program where they already look. The new CLAUDE.md invariant stops a later editor from moving the define mechanics back into model prose. This is the largest edit, spread over six or more files and one runtime skill, so the hosts rebuild is required. It fixes the count "two" into prose, and that goes stale again when a third tool arrives. Some wording, such as whether the open-question tool is still the only code that writes `open_questions.xml` and whether CONTRIBUTING's test-suite paragraph covers both tools, depends on how the code-reuse and test-suite questions are settled.

Edit only the statements the new tool makes false: CLAUDE.md's "one stdlib-only Python tool" sentence and its layout block, CONTRIBUTING.md's "the one program", and the docs/skill-reference.md `define-milestone-goal` entry, which describes `create`-first ordering the tool replaces. Leave the bootstrap justification and docs/workflow.md alone. They describe the open-question tool's role accurately, and `python3` is still required whichever tool asks for it. This is the smallest diff that leaves the documentation correct. It avoids touching the bootstrap SKILL.md, a runtime file whose check and remedy don't change at all. A reader of the bootstrap or docs/workflow.md never learns that milestone definition also runs Python, so the justification for the prerequisite is incomplete. Whether the docs/workflow.md sentence about the question document's one writer is still true depends on how the code-reuse question is settled, so the unedited surfaces may need a second look later anyway.

open-question.question: Do the requirements.md, TASKS_TODO.md, and TASKS_DONE.md templates move out of the skill's prose into the tool source, so SKILL.md no longer states any file contents, or does the skill keep them as documentation?
open-question.recommendation: The tool becomes the one source of the file contents and the runtime skill carries only what its runner still needs, which is the no-editor-facing-prose rule the open-question skills already follow for the rendered document, so no prose copy or summary can drift from what the tool writes; the section headings other skills rely on stay described in CLAUDE.md's milestone file structure and pinned by the tool's tests, and separate template files would add non-Python files to core/tools/ with a load step and a new failure mode.
open-question.alternative: The three Markdown templates live only as string constants in core/tools/define_milestone.py. SKILL.md names the four files the tool creates and states none of their contents. The section layout that other skills rely on stays described where it already is: CLAUDE.md's milestone file structure, docs/skill-reference.md, and the tool's own tests. There is one source of truth for the file contents. The runtime skill carries only what its runner still needs, which follows the no-editor-facing-prose invariant and matches how the open-question skills treat open_questions.xml, whose rendered form lives only in the tool. It also leaves no second copy that can drift from what the tool actually writes. Specify-milestone-starting-state, review-milestone-requirements, derive-tasks and modify-milestone-goal depend on those headings (## Relevant starting state, ## Decisions, ## Out of Scope, # TASKS TODO). Once this lands, the exact skeleton is visible only by reading Python source or a golden test fixture. A contributor who changes a heading in the tool gets no prompt in the skill layer to check those skills.

The tool holds the templates verbatim. SKILL.md adds one sentence naming what the files contain (the numbered title heading, the goal under ## Goal, the three empty sections, and the two TASKS headings) but no code blocks, and does not say how the files are written. The skill stays mechanical and states no byte-level contents that could drift, but a reader of the skill still sees the section contract that downstream skills rely on without opening the tool source. The one sentence still restates part of the tool's output in prose and is not checked against the tool, so it can quietly drift when the tool changes. A runner that no longer writes the files also gains nothing from it, which puts it close to the editor-facing prose the runtime-file invariant keeps out of SKILL.md.

The tool holds the templates as the executable source. SKILL.md keeps its current requirements.md, TASKS_TODO.md and TASKS_DONE.md code blocks unchanged, labelled as documentation of what the tool writes. A test under tests/ could optionally pull those blocks out of SKILL.md and compare them with the tool's output. The change is smallest and loses the least information. Anyone reading the skill sees exactly what a new milestone looks like, in the same place as today, and an optional sync test could catch drift mechanically. The same text lives in two places. Without the sync test, the SKILL.md copy is a second source that no step uses and that can go stale unnoticed. With the test, the suite starts reading runtime Markdown prose, a new kind of coupling it doesn't have today. Either way the runner loads contents it must not act on, which cuts against a fully mechanical skill.

The three skeletons move into plain Markdown template files next to the tool under core/tools/ (for example a templates/ subdirectory). The tool locates them from its own file path and fills in the number, title and goal. SKILL.md states no contents. There is one source of truth that stays readable as Markdown rather than as Python string literals, so a contributor can see and edit the milestone skeleton directly without touching code or keeping a copy in the skill. It adds non-Python files to core/tools/. The host build renders them into both host trees and runs its text checks on them (no bare {{, no host name). The tool then needs a file-location step and a new failure mode for a missing or unreadable template. It is also a placeholder-substitution scheme that the stdlib-only single-module tools don't use today, and it spreads one tool's behaviour across several files.

open-question.question: What counts as a conflict the tool refuses on, beyond the target directory already existing: a slug already used under another number, the same number under another slug, or a non-directory entry at the target path?
open-question.recommendation: With max-plus-one numbering over a scan that counts every milestone-shaped directory under any padding, no directory can already hold the computed number, so the only clash left is an entry at the exact target path, and an exclusive create catches that atomically with no check-then-create race; a second pass over the root would be defensive code that fires only for a stray file, and slug uniqueness would add a retry loop to a mechanical skill for a name derived from the title's first words.
open-question.alternative: The only conflict check is creating the target directory exclusively (a create that fails if anything already sits at the path, rather than one that tolerates an existing directory). Any existing entry at `milestones/milestone_<NN>_<slug>`, whether a directory, a file, or a symlink, becomes the one `Error:` line. A slug reused under another number and the same number under another slug are both allowed. It is the smallest rule and the hardest to get wrong. The filesystem enforces it atomically, so no race between checking and creating is possible. With max-plus-one numbering, a clash can only come from an entry the scan missed, and this still catches every such entry at the exact target path. It also refuses before anything is written, so nothing is left behind. It drops the guard the skill has today: step 3 refuses a number already taken under any slug. An entry the scan ignores could then leave two milestones sharing one number, for example a stray `milestone_38_x` file, a differently padded `milestone_038_y`, or a non-matching name. Two directories with the same number would break `goto-next-milestone`'s lowest-undone pick and the history headings keyed on the number. How much this matters depends on which names the number scan counts.

Before writing, the tool refuses in two cases. The first is anything already at the target path, of any kind. The second is any entry in the milestones root, directory or not and under any padding, whose zero-stripped number equals the computed one under a different slug. Slug reuse under another number stays allowed. It keeps the skill's current number-uniqueness guarantee, which `goto-next-milestone` and the `### Milestone N — Title` history rely on to identify a milestone. It also closes the gap between what the scan counts and what exists on disk, and it adds no rule the workflow does not already need. Slug reuse is harmless because every consumer addresses a milestone by its full directory path or its number. It needs a second pass over the root with its own looser name matching, beside the number scan's matching, and the two must stay consistent. Under max-plus-one numbering this check almost never fires, so it is mostly defensive code that still needs its own tests and fixtures. Because it is a separate check before an exclusive create, it still needs the create to fail safely if something appears at the path in between.

This keeps both refusals from the target-path-and-number option and adds a third. The tool also refuses when the derived slug already names an existing milestone under any other number. Every milestone then has a unique number and a unique slug. A repeated slug is most likely a repeated or near-duplicate goal, and this surfaces it at definition time. It keeps directory names unambiguous to humans reading `milestones/` and git history, where the `Milestone-definition:` subjects would otherwise repeat a descriptor. None of the 37 existing slugs repeats, so the rule rejects nothing today. The slug is now derived mechanically from the title's first five words, so different goals with similar titles will collide, especially generic openings. The only fix is for the model to pick a different title, which adds a retry loop to a skill meant to be mechanical. That loop blocks a headless `claude -p` chain. How often it fires depends on how the slug normalization handles stop words and truncation.
